terms: The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.
A cell with a nucleus enclosed in a membrane; e.g. animal, plant, fungus cells.
A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.
Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.
Addition of methyl groups to cytosine, generally suppressing gene transcription.
Heritable changes in gene expression without altering DNA base sequence, via DNA methylation and histone modification.
Process by which information from a gene leads to a functional product (protein or RNA).
Mutated proto-oncogene whose product drives uncontrolled cell division, contributing to tumour formation.
Undifferentiated cell capable of self-renewal and differentiation; totipotent, pluripotent or multipotent.
Protein that binds to DNA, switching genes on or off by promoting or blocking RNA polymerase.
Energy passed to next trophic level as a percentage; about 10% between consumers, lower for producers.
Enrichment of waters with nutrients causing algal blooms, decomposition by bacteria and O₂ depletion.
NPP = GPP − R, energy available to next trophic level after respiratory losses.
Cycling of nitrogen via fixation (Rhizobium), nitrification (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter), denitrification and decomposition.
Autotroph that converts light or chemical energy into biomass; e.g. plants, algae.
A feeding level within an ecosystem; producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers, etc.
Triplet of bases on mRNA that codes for one amino acid or a stop signal.
Triplet, degenerate, non-overlapping and universal sequence of bases in DNA that codes for amino acids.
Non-coding section of a eukaryotic gene removed by splicing of the primary mRNA transcript.
Synthesis of mRNA from a DNA template by RNA polymerase in the nucleus.
Synthesis of polypeptide at a ribosome from mRNA; tRNA brings amino acids matching codons.
Transfer RNA carrying a specific amino acid and bearing an anticodon complementary to an mRNA codon.
Proportion of a given allele in the gene pool, expressed as a decimal or percentage.
Sharp reduction in population size that reduces genetic diversity and changes allele frequencies.
Total of all alleles of all genes in a population at a given time.
Random change in allele frequency, more pronounced in small populations.
p² + 2pq + q² = 1; estimates genotype frequencies when no evolutionary forces act on a population.
Group of individuals of the same species in the same area at the same time who can interbreed.
Microscopic air sacs in the lungs providing a large, thin, moist surface for gas exchange.
Blood and water flow in opposite directions across fish gills, maintaining a diffusion gradient along the entire length.
Pores on plant leaves (mostly underside) flanked by guard cells, regulating gas exchange and water loss.
Higher in small organisms, allowing exchange across body surface; falls with size, requiring specialised systems.
Branching air tubes in insects delivering oxygen directly to tissues; close via spiracles.
Movement of air (or water) over the gas exchange surface to maintain steep diffusion gradients.
A non-directional response in which an organism changes its rate of movement or turning according to the intensity of a non-directional stimulus.
A specialised cell or sensory ending that detects a specific stimulus and acts as a transducer, converting it into a nerve impulse.
The neurone pathway receptor to sensory to relay to motor to effector that produces a rapid, automatic, protective response without conscious thought.
A detectable change in the internal or external environment of an organism that can bring about a response giving a survival advantage.
A directional movement of a simple motile organism either towards (positive) or away from (negative) a directional stimulus such as light.
A growth response of a plant in which the direction of growth is determined by the direction of a stimulus, for example phototropism towards light.
Reaction joining monomers and releasing water
Covalent bond between two sugar monomers
Reaction splitting polymers by adding water
Small repeating unit (e.g. glucose, amino acid, nucleotide)
Long chain of monomers joined by condensation
Isomers differing in OH position on C1 — gives starch vs cellulose
Different version of a gene producing different forms of the same characteristic.
Section of DNA coding for one polypeptide (or functional RNA); occupies a specific locus on a chromosome.
Having two different alleles at a locus (e.g. Aa).
Having two identical alleles at a locus (e.g. AA or aa).
Differential survival and reproduction of organisms due to phenotypic variation; favourable alleles increase in frequency.
Observable characteristics resulting from interaction of genotype and environment.
Joining of two molecules with loss of water and formation of a new chemical bond.
Bond between glycerol and a fatty acid in triglycerides, formed by condensation.
Covalent bond between two sugar molecules formed by condensation.
Breaking of a bond by addition of water; reverse of condensation.
Small repeating subunit that forms polymers, e.g. amino acid, monosaccharide, nucleotide.
Large molecule formed from many monomers joined by condensation reactions.
Variety of living organisms; measured at species, genetic and ecosystem levels.
Ex situ conservation; breeding endangered species in captivity to maintain gene pools and reintroduce them.
Protection and management of habitats and species to maintain biodiversity for future generations.
D = 1 − Σ(n/N)², a measure of biodiversity including both richness and evenness.
Relative abundance of different species in a community; high if abundances are similar.
The number of different species in a community, ignoring relative abundance.
Steroid? No: catecholamine secreted by adrenal medulla; activates fight-or-flight, raising heart rate and blood glucose.
Ductless gland secreting hormones directly into the blood, e.g. pituitary, thyroid, pancreas.
Peptide hormone from α cells of pancreas; raises blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Chemical messenger secreted into the bloodstream and acting on target cells with complementary receptors.
Peptide hormone from β cells of pancreas; lowers blood glucose by stimulating uptake and glycogenesis.
Intracellular molecule (e.g. cAMP) that relays a signal from a hormone-receptor binding to enzymes inside the cell.
Variables kept constant during an experiment to ensure a fair test.
Variable measured to detect the effect of the independent variable.
Variable deliberately changed by the investigator to test its effect.
Consistency of measurements; improved by repeats and calculating means.
Data should be recorded with appropriate precision and correct SI units throughout.
Whether the data measure what the experiment claims; ensured by controlling variables and removing bias.
All living organisms are composed of cells; cells are the smallest unit of life; cells arise from pre-existing cells (Schleiden, Schwann 1838-39; Virchow 1858).
Mitochondria and chloroplasts originated from free-living prokaryotes engulfed by ancestral eukaryotes (Margulis 1967).
Cell with membrane-bound nucleus and organelles; includes protists, fungi, plants, animals.
Phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins; selectively permeable (Singer & Nicolson 1972).
Cell without membrane-bound nucleus or organelles; DNA in nucleoid; includes bacteria and archaea.
As cells grow, volume increases faster than surface area, limiting diffusion; drives mitotic division.
Cell with nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, 80S ribosomes
Modifies, packages and labels proteins into vesicles
Vesicle of hydrolytic enzymes — breaks down waste
Cell with no nucleus, 70S ribosomes, circular DNA — e.g. bacteria
Studded with ribosomes — synthesises and folds proteins
No ribosomes — synthesises lipids and steroids

Adds free DNA nucleotides 5' to 3', complementary to template
Enzyme unwinding the double helix at the replication fork

Synthesised continuously towards the replication fork
Each new helix has one parent + one new strand
Normal light nitrogen — incorporated by new DNA
Heavy isotope of nitrogen used to label parental DNA
Hypothesis: both strands of one daughter molecule are old
Ultracentrifugation technique that separates DNA by density
Hypothesis: both strands are a mix of old and new fragments
Each new DNA molecule contains one parent + one new strand

Community + abiotic environment, with energy flow and nutrient cycles

Relative abundance of different species in a community; high if abundances are similar.

Movement of molecules or ions across a membrane against a concentration gradient, requiring carrier proteins and energy from ATP.
A membrane channel protein that transports chloride ions; a faulty version disrupts water movement and produces abnormally thick mucus.
A person with one normal and one faulty recessive allele who shows no symptoms but can pass the faulty allele to offspring.
A recessive genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the CFTR gene, producing faulty chloride channels and thick, sticky mucus in the lungs and gut.
A treatment that delivers a working copy of a gene, for example using a liposome or virus vector, into cells to correct a genetic disorder.
Testing DNA to detect alleles associated with genetic conditions, used in prenatal, carrier or pre-implantation contexts and raising ethical issues.
A rapid reversal of membrane potential, depolarising to about +40 mV, that travels along an axon once a threshold stimulus is reached.
The ability of the brain to change its structure and neural connections in response to experience, learning or damage.
Retinal cells that function in bright light, allow colour vision through three types and give high visual acuity at the fovea.
A specialised nerve cell that conducts electrical impulses, consisting of dendrites, a cell body and an axon often insulated by a myelin sheath.
Light-sensitive cells in the retina that work in dim light, give monochrome vision and show high sensitivity but low visual acuity.
A junction between two neurones where a neurotransmitter is released, diffuses across the gap and stimulates receptors on the next cell.
Y-shaped glycoprotein with variable region complementary to a specific antigen; agglutinates pathogens.
Molecule (usually protein) on a pathogen surface that triggers an immune response.
Lymphocyte that, when activated, divides and differentiates into plasma cells producing antibodies.
Long-lived lymphocyte produced after primary response, enabling rapid secondary response on re-infection.
Engulfing of pathogens by phagocytes; vesicle fuses with lysosome to digest the pathogen.
Recognises antigens presented on APCs, releases cytokines to stimulate B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
A plaque of cholesterol, fibrous tissue and cell debris in an artery wall that can rupture and trigger a blood clot (thrombosis).
The build-up of fatty deposits (atheroma) in artery walls, narrowing the lumen and reducing blood flow, which raises cardiovascular disease risk.
A correlation shows two variables change together, but does not by itself prove that one variable causes the change in the other.
A lipoprotein that carries cholesterol from tissues back to the liver, helping to lower blood cholesterol and reduce cardiovascular risk.
A lipoprotein that carries cholesterol to body cells; high blood LDL levels are associated with the formation of atheroma in arteries.
A variable linked with an increased probability of disease, such as smoking, high blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol or physical inactivity.
All the living organisms (biotic factors) and non-living conditions (abiotic factors) interacting in an area, through which energy flows and nutrients cycle.
The warming of Earth's surface caused by gases such as carbon dioxide and methane absorbing and re-emitting infrared radiation.
The total rate at which producers convert light energy into chemical energy in organic compounds by photosynthesis, per unit area per unit time.
The chemical energy stored by producers after subtracting energy lost in respiration; the energy available to the next trophic level.
The formation of new species when populations become reproductively isolated and diverge through natural selection or genetic drift.
The directional change in a community over time, from a pioneer community through seral stages to a stable climax community.
The immediate energy currency of cells; its hydrolysis to ADP and inorganic phosphate releases energy that powers muscle contraction.
The complete oxidation of glucose using oxygen in the mitochondria, releasing a large yield of ATP plus carbon dioxide and water.
Respiration without oxygen that produces lactate in muscle, giving a small but rapid ATP yield and causing an oxygen debt.
The extra oxygen taken in after exercise to oxidise the lactate that built up during anaerobic respiration.
The functional contractile unit of a myofibril, running between two Z-lines and containing overlapping actin and myosin filaments.
Muscle contraction in which myosin heads bind actin and pull the thin filaments past the thick filaments, shortening each sarcomere.
The release of enzymes from the sperm's acrosome that digest the egg's outer layers, allowing one sperm to fertilise the egg.
The process by which an unspecialised cell becomes specialised by switching particular genes on or off to make specific proteins.
A haploid sex cell, sperm or egg, produced by meiosis that fuses with another gamete at fertilisation to restore the diploid number.
A reduction division producing four genetically varied haploid cells, generating variation through crossing over and independent assortment.
An undifferentiated cell that can divide and differentiate into specialised cell types; it may be totipotent, pluripotent or multipotent.
A protein that binds to DNA and switches genes on or off, controlling which proteins a cell makes and therefore its phenotype.
